evidence: Suet. Aug. 23 (Lewis & Short, s.v. praeses: prōvinciārum, governors)
terms.comment: Properly a guardian or one who presides; from Augustus on, the general word for the governor of a province, whatever his rank (the jurists in the Digest; Lewis & Short). Modern Latin also uses praeses for a president (see president), so say whose governor: praeses prōvinciae.

terms.gloss: the ruler of a province, governor
evidence: Tac. Ann. 2.4; Suet. Aug. 89 (Lewis & Short, s.v. rēctor)

terms.gloss: proconsul: a governor with a consul’s powers
terms.comment: The Republican title of a former consul sent to govern a province; for a Roman governor, not a modern one.

terms.gloss: governor (of a colony or a modern state)
evidence: M-O s.v. governor (Turselinus 1652; Way 1771, of a colonial governor of Pennsylvania)
terms.comment: Classically a helmsman, and so figuratively a guide of the state: custōdēs gubernātōrēsque reī pūblicae (Cic. Rab. Perd. 26; Lewis & Short). Later Latin made it the title of royal and colonial governors (Morgan–Owens).

evidence: Lewis & Short s.v. prōcūrātor: of the governors of small provinces under the emperors

phrases.latin: Praeses prōvinciae crās in oppidum veniet.
phrases.english: The governor of the province is coming to the town tomorrow.
